Honestly, I don't think there is a good solution; inconsistent data cannot be meaningfully merged

Something that might be fixable is the inconsistency in the output when faced with mismatched inputs. We keep the "first" set of branches when there's a mismatch; if the order changes between runs, then we can end up with a different result.

I agree, inconsistency data cannot be merged.

Having said that, I understand the solution for this is hard, but choosing the first set does not sound like a final solution to me. I'm not exepert in code coverage in C++ to say how this is resolved in other environments, I don't think this is a Bazel problem but a more generic one.
If you grab the example in the ticket and you apply it to a real life scenario, you can imagine that `baz` is the object file that instantiated the header for testing it with all possible instantiations you might have in the project.
In that case, what the user might want is to grab the set of branches from `baz` but taking the first you are just relying on lack.

One way to mitigate the problem is to use some tool like gcovr to exclude branches generated by the compiler.
https://gcovr.com/en/stable/faq.html#why-does-c-code-have-so-many-uncovered-branches
In the end, I would expect that most of the users when they want to test different branches they care mainly about the branches that are visible in the C++ code.

Maybe a flag where you can choose between taking the first set or throw an exception would be the best? Do you see a way how a user could in practice influence how the first set of branches is choosen?

issue.title: Fix: malformed brda records caused bad branching coverage

labels.name: awaiting-review
labels.description: PR is awaiting review from an assigned reviewer

repository.name: bazel
repository.description: a fast, scalable, multi-language and extensible build system

issue.body:
While working on a large bazel migration project in Volvo Cars, I noticed that for merged coverage reports (i.e. `bazel coverage target1 target2 ... targetN) bazel would generate different branch coverage on each run. It would also be very inflated compared to running the same in our pre-bazel environment. This essentially made it unusable.

After much detective work it turns out that individual tests in bazel can create malformed BRDA records where the same unique branch (i.e. the same, line, block and branch) have multiple values. When this happens the coverageOutputGenerator simply adds all the incorrect records to the merged file. In the merging logic there are some checks that sometimes drops individual records based on the order in which the BRDA records have been merged. Given that bazel does not guarantee that order, this then leads to each run having different branch coverage. 

E.g. 
Bazel has generated this (counted as 6 branches)
BRDA:131,0,0,1
BRDA:131,0,1,1
BRDA:131,0,0,1
BRDA:131,0,1,0
BRDA:131,0,0,3
BRDA:131,0,1,1

Which should've been only this (counted as 2 branches):
BRDA:131,0,1,2
BRDA:131,0,0,5

This fix ensures that each branch is unique for a particular source file. Duplicates are now merged, ensuring that the tally is correct. I have verified that this works consistently on our large code base and added some regression tests to avoid this bug in the future.
